title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
directAnswer: Keep each value at most twice, in-place, and return the new length k. Because the array is sorted, duplicates are contiguous, so a single write pointer suffices: write nums[fast] only when k < 2 OR nums[fast] != nums[k-2]. That comparison against the element two slots back is the whole trick — it caps every run at two. O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Sorted input is the load-bearing assumption** — it makes equal values contiguous, so a length-2 look-back bounds the whole run.
Generalises instantly: for 'keep at most m', compare to `nums[k-m]`.
Return `k`; the judge reads only `nums[0..k)` and ignores the tail.

remember.takeaway: When the array is sorted, 'at most m copies' becomes a one-line write-pointer rule: keep nums[fast] iff it differs from nums[k-m]. The sortedness turns a counting problem into a constant look-back — generalize the index offset and you've solved the whole family.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you exploit sortedness to avoid counting structures, and whether you can express 'at most two' as a clean invariant on the write pointer rather than ad-hoc counters.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing nums[fast] against nums[fast-1] in the original array (breaks once you start overwriting), or using a separate run-counter that mishandles the boundary between values.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the nums[k-2] invariant and immediately generalize: 'for at most m, compare to nums[k-m]'. Note that sortedness is the assumption that makes a length-2 window sufficient.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums` sorted in **non-decreasing order**, remove some duplicates **in-place** such that each unique element appears **at most twice**. The relative order of the elements should be kept the same.

Since it is impossible to change the length of the array in some languages, you must instead have the result be placed in the first part of the array `nums`. More formally, if there are `k` elements after removing the duplicates, then the first `k` elements of `nums` should hold the final result. It does not matter what you leave beyond the first `k` elements.

Return `k` after placing the final result in the first `k` slots of `nums`.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
understanding: Compact the sorted array so no value appears more than twice, preserving order, and return the new length k. Because equal values sit next to each other, you only need to check whether adding the current element would create a third copy.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the input guaranteed sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, non-decreasing. That's essential — it makes duplicates contiguous so a fixed-size look-back bounds each run. On unsorted input the look-back trick fails.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must I preserve the relative order of the kept elements?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes (unlike Remove Element). The write pointer naturally preserves order since it copies left to right.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about the elements after index k?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Don't-cares. The grader only inspects nums[0..k); leftover values past k are fine.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the array have just one element?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, length ≥ 1. A single element is trivially fine — k = 1, and the k < 2 guard handles it.

approaches.name: Explicit Run Counter (Intuitive First Pass)
approaches.whenToMention: Good to sketch first to show you understand the requirement, then refine to the look-back form. Don't present this as your final answer — it's wordier and error-prone at boundaries.
hints: Walk the array and track the value of the current run and how many times you've already kept it. When do you write versus skip?
Keep a write pointer k, the previous value, and a count. If the current value equals the previous, increment count; otherwise reset count to 1.
Write the element only while count <= 2. Reset the counter whenever the value changes.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass, constant bookkeeping (k, prev, count) → O(n) time, O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Before the slick one-liner, it helps to write the requirement out literally: as you scan, remember which value you're currently in a run of, and how many copies of it you've already committed. Keep writing copies until you've placed two, then suppress the rest until a new value appears.

**Why a counter feels natural but is fiddly.** The logic 'count up to 2, then reset on value change' is the direct reading of the problem, and it works. But it carries three pieces of state — the write pointer `k`, the previous value `prev`, and the run `count` — and the reset has to happen at exactly the right moment. Off-by-one bugs cluster around 'do I reset before or after writing?' and 'what's the initial count?'. It's correct, just heavier than it needs to be.

**Why it's still worth saying out loud.** Verbalizing this version proves to the interviewer that you understand *what* must hold (no third copy) independent of the clever encoding. The optimal solution then lands as a simplification — you replace three variables with a single comparison — which reads as insight rather than memorization.

**The bridge to the optimal.** Notice that `count` and `prev` together just answer one question: *would writing this element create a third identical copy?* On sorted data, that's answerable directly from the array we're already building — if the slot two back (`nums[k-2]`) holds the same value, we'd be making a third. That observation collapses all the bookkeeping into one condition.
approaches.insight: The run counter and the previous-value tracker are redundant on sorted data — the array you're constructing already remembers both. Spotting that redundancy is the step from 'works' to 'elegant'.

approaches.name: Write Pointer with Look-Back-by-2 (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Lead with the invariant — 'keep nums[fast] iff it differs from nums[k-2]' — and mention it generalizes to nums[k-m] for 'at most m'.
hints: The array you're writing into is also sorted. If the element two slots back equals the current element, what does that tell you about how many copies you've already kept?
Maintain a write pointer k. Accept nums[fast] when k < 2 (first two slots always fit) or when nums[fast] != nums[k-2].
If nums[fast] == nums[k-2], the slots k-2 and k-1 already hold two copies of this value, so writing a third is forbidden — skip it.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Single pass with one comparison and at most one write per element → O(n) time. Only the write pointer k as extra state → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Because the input is sorted, the prefix we're building in `nums[0..k)` is also sorted. That lets us answer 'have I already kept two of this value?' by peeking at a single slot rather than maintaining counters.

**The invariant, stated precisely.** At all times, `nums[0..k)` is a valid answer for the elements processed so far — every value appears at most twice. To extend it with the current element `x = nums[fast]`, we ask: would this create a *third* copy? Since the prefix is sorted, if `x` is going to collide it must collide with the largest values already kept, which live at `nums[k-1]` and `nums[k-2]`. If both equal `x`, then `nums[k-2] == x`, and accepting `x` would make three. So the accept rule is exactly **`k < 2 || x != nums[k-2]`**.

**Why comparing to `nums[k-2]` and not `nums[fast-1]`.** A tempting bug is to compare against the previous element in the *original* array. But we're overwriting `nums` as we go, so the original neighbors get clobbered — and more importantly, the count we care about is how many copies we've *kept*, which lives in the compacted prefix, not the raw input. The `k-2` slot is the authoritative record of 'the second-most-recent value I committed'. If even *that* equals `x`, we're already at two.

**Why `k < 2` comes first.** For the first two writes there is no `nums[k-2]` to read (it'd be a negative index). Short-circuit evaluation makes `k < 2` accept those unconditionally — the first two elements of any array are always allowed, since you can't exceed two copies with fewer than three slots filled. This also elegantly removes the need for the length-≤-2 special case the counter version needed.

**Why it generalizes for free.** Nothing about the value `2` is special. 'Keep at most `m` copies' becomes 'accept iff `k < m` or `x != nums[k-m]`'. The look-back distance *is* the multiplicity cap. Saying this in an interview signals you understand the structure, not just this instance.
approaches.insight: On sorted data, the compacted prefix is a self-documenting counter: nums[k-2] == x means 'two copies of x already committed'. Replace explicit counting with a fixed-distance look-back, and the offset equals the multiplicity you allow.

diagrams.title: Look-back-by-2 capping a run
diagrams.caption: When nums[fast] equals nums[k-2], two copies are already committed, so we skip.

edgeCases.behavior: First two accepted via k<2; third has nums[k-2]=nums[0]=1 → skip → k=2.

pitfalls: Comparing nums[fast] to nums[fast-1] instead of nums[k-2] — wrong once overwriting begins.
Dropping the k < 2 guard — negative index into nums[-2] (Java throws, Python silently wraps).
Hard-coding 2 when the follow-up asks for m — remember the offset is the cap.

commonMistakes: Comparing against the original previous element (nums[fast-1]) rather than the kept slot nums[k-2].
Omitting the k < 2 guard and indexing out of bounds.
Using a hash map to count — works but wastes O(unique) space on already-sorted data.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing to the wrong slot
commonMistakesDetailed.why: nums[fast-1] reads the original (now possibly overwritten) array and tracks input adjacency, not how many copies you've KEPT. The authoritative count lives in the compacted prefix at nums[k-2].

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the k < 2 short-circuit
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Evaluating nums[k-2] when k is 0 or 1 reads nums[-2]/nums[-1]. Java throws ArrayIndexOutOfBounds; Python silently reads from the end and corrupts the logic.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Resetting the run counter to 0 instead of 1
commonMistakesDetailed.why: In the explicit-counter variant, a new value has already been seen once, so its count must start at 1. Resetting to 0 makes you keep three copies (0,1,2 all <= 2 before the cap kicks in).

patternNote: Look-back-by-m write pointer for in-place dedupe on sorted arrays. Recognise it whenever you must cap each value's multiplicity with O(1) space. The offset m is the cap: m = 1 is LC 26, m = 2 is this problem.
